items.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Wilbert Harrison’s version of Kansas City.

ctx.x: Not really. A good shuffle, when it’s right in the pocket is, oh man. I can’t remember, you just gave me an idea, a thought. I was driving home one day many years ago and I was listening to like a light rock station. And I heard the beginning of what almost sounded like the beginning of “Spirit in the Sky” but that wasn’t the recording. But the band in the background went [scats] just that, the bass player and the guitar player. And every once in a while someone would lean in and say, “Mercy” and then [scats].…

Yeah. It’s so fascinating. I’ve been obsessed with the — I don’t know if it’s the actual original but Wilbert Harrison’s version of Kansas City. If you listen to that, it’s so perfect and it just drives, and I can’t even imagine the recording technology at that time but there’s something about it. There’s this chunk-a-chunk-a-chunk-a-chunk. You can’t even recognize the instrument. But I’m not sure where I’m going with this but boy when things work they just are awesome.

The greatest break on drums in rock & roll has been played all kinds of different ways and by all kinds of different people. Most folks remember it from Phil Collins and a couple of the albums he did because he always did double stops on it. He would play something on the drumset, then he would play it again backing himself up so it would sound like three, four, five guys at the same time. But there was a groove by a gentleman by the name of Junior Walker and his band Junior Walker and the All-Stars.
